title: The collect for peace (1662)
hookLine: give unto thy servants that peace which the world cannot give
tomorrow: what do you say standing at the edge of a grave?
last: ALL THE BLESSINGS OF THIS LIFE.

cards: Noise-canceling headphones, a do-not-disturb setting, a quiet room booked for an hour: peace you can buy or arrange.

Evening Prayer in the 1662 prayer book ends with three short prayers, and the second asks for something odd. Not a quieter street, not a calmer week. It asks God for "that peace which the world cannot give."
And here's the strange detail: before it asks for peace at all, it talks about desires, counsels and works.

teach.b: A collect is a short, set prayer, and this one has a shape you can see. It doesn't start by asking.
It starts by naming where good things come from: "O God, from whom all holy desires, all good counsels, and all just works do proceed: Give unto thy servants that peace which the world cannot give."

Desires, counsels, works: wanting the good, choosing it, doing it. All three, it says, start with God. That's the puzzle's first answer: the peace comes from the same place as wanting the good at all.
At the Last Supper in John's Gospel, Jesus tells his friends: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you." The collect turns that into a request.
Then it says what the peace is for: hearts set to obey God's commandments, and, defended from the fear of enemies, time passed in rest and quietness. Look at the order.
One way Christians read it: the world's peace arrives when the trouble leaves.
This prayer asks for a peace that can come first, while the trouble is still in the room.

how: In the 1662 prayer book this collect is said near the end of Evening Prayer, and Anglican and Episcopal churches still pray it, or a version of it, at evening services.

games.q: what does “the collect for peace” mean?
o: a prayer for a peace God gives, not circumstances
a church collection taken up for peacemakers
a treaty prayer read when wars end

s: in this prayer, peace means nothing is going wrong
the likely reading. it asks for a peace given by God, even before the trouble leaves.
the phrase borrows from Jesus' words in John's Gospel
my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth.
the collect starts by asking for peace right away

games.q: the night before a big exam, your friend has tried everything: a playlist, a clean desk, phone in a drawer. still no peace. what would the collect add?
o: a better playlist; peace is about the right setup.
a peace asked for, given even with the exam still there.
skipping the exam until things calm down.
games.why: the collect asks for that peace which the world cannot give; in its order, the rest and quietness come last.

practice: Walk slowly across the room and back as the sit begins. With each step, bring to mind one place where peace feels thin, a conversation, a worry, a person, and let the phrase walk beside it: peace which the world cannot give.
Sit when you're ready; if you pray, you can say the collect's line once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: The collect for peace. The prayer book's evening request for a peace that's given, not arranged.

orig.note: Greek for peace, the word in John's Gospel when Jesus says my peace I give unto you.

carryVoice: Your line: peace the world cannot give, the kind that can arrive before the trouble leaves. Goodnight.
